subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Mentoring programme, session notes. Written by Vasudha, mentor.
Pooja (25), four months into the strategy team. Asked how meetings were going, she said, 'Fine. I mostly listen.'
When I pushed a little, it came out in a rush. 'Everyone in that room talks like they already know the answer. Rohit quotes numbers from memory. Sheetal just says, "Obviously we should…" and people nod. Inside I'm checking my point five times, and by the time I'm sure, the meeting has moved on.'
She said she'd had an idea about the pricing slide on Tuesday, and someone else said something similar ten minutes later, and it went into the plan. 'So maybe it wasn't special. Maybe I'm just not adding much.'
She laughed when she said it, but she didn't look up.
Next session: we'll talk about how everyone's outside looks, compared with her own inside. And one small point to say aloud next week.

qa.q: What did Pooja have an idea about on Tuesday?
qa.a: She had an idea about the pricing slide.

qa.q: What does Pooja believe about her place in the team, and what shows it?
qa.a: She feels discouraged and unsure she adds much, which shows when she says, 'Maybe I'm just not adding much,' without looking up.

qa.q: What small step could Pooja try to break the pattern of silence?
qa.a: She could say one point aloud early in a meeting, even before she is fully sure, so her ideas are heard and credited.

qa.q: How might Rohit and Sheetal look from their side of the table, compared with how Pooja sees them?
qa.a: They may have their own doubts too; Pooja only sees their confident outside, not whatever uncertainty they feel inside.

grounding: It shows a new hire comparing her inner doubts with colleagues' outer confidence, staying silent, and then taking her invisibility as proof she adds little.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Wed, 11 pm
Same thing again today. Client call at four, eight of us on the screen. Nikita presented the market sizing like she was born doing it. Not one 'um'. The partner kept nodding.
I had a point about the rural distribution costs. I'd even checked it twice. I kept my mic on mute, waiting for the right moment, rehearsing the sentence. The moment didn't come. Or it came and I let it go.
At the end the partner said, 'Good session, team.' Nobody mentioned me because there was nothing to mention.
It's week nine. I think they've already filed me as the quiet one. Maybe that's accurate. Maybe the others just think faster.
Everyone else looks so sure. I'm sure they don't lie awake like this.
Tomorrow: internal review. I'll probably stay quiet there too.
— Gautam

qa.q: How many people were on the screen for the client call?
qa.a: Eight of us were on the screen for the client call.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling after the call, and what shows it?
qa.a: Gautam felt invisible and doubtful, writing that there was nothing to mention and that maybe the others just think faster.

qa.q: What small change could Gautam try in tomorrow's internal review?
qa.a: Gautam could share the rural distribution point in the first few minutes, since it was already checked twice, instead of waiting for a perfect moment.

qa.q: How might Nikita see her own presentation, compared with how Gautam sees it?
qa.a: Nikita may have felt nervous or rushed inside, even though from outside Gautam only saw confidence.

grounding: It shows a new hire comparing inner doubt with a colleague's outer confidence and staying silent, then treating that invisibility as proof of adding little.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
"You had the answer in the meeting," Sumit said, sliding into the canteen chair. "I saw you write it down."
"What answer?"
"About the vendor delay. You wrote 'check the customs date' on your pad. Then Neha said the same thing ten minutes later and the boss loved it."
"She said it better."
"She said it louder."
Vikas stirred his dal. "Everyone in that room sounds so sure. Neha, Prakash, even the intern. I sit there thinking, if I say something wrong, they'll all know I don't belong."
"You think they're never unsure?"
"They don't look it."
"And you don't look unsure either. You look silent. That's all anyone sees."
"Great. So now I'm the guy who adds nothing."
"You're the guy who had the answer first."
Vikas didn't reply. He pushed the rice around, the notepad folded in his shirt pocket.

qa.q: What did Vikas write on his pad?
qa.a: Check the customs date.

qa.q: What is Vikas afraid of when he stays silent in meetings?
qa.a: He is afraid and insecure that one wrong comment will expose him as not belonging among confident colleagues.

qa.q: What small step could Vikas take in the next meeting?
qa.a: Say one of his written points aloud early, like the customs date, before anyone else does.

qa.q: How does Sumit see Vikas's silence?
qa.a: Sumit sees a capable colleague hiding good ideas, and seems frustrated that others only see silence.

grounding: A young employee measures his private doubts against colleagues' confident fronts, stays silent, and becomes invisible.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Four months into the agency, I've noticed something about myself I don't like. In every review, Avni talks first. She says things like, "I'm not sure, but what if the logo had more space?" and everyone leans in. I sit there with three ideas in my notebook and a voice in my head saying they're obvious, or wrong, or both.
I compare my inside, which is all doubt, with everyone else's outside, which looks like confidence. It isn't a fair match, but it doesn't feel unfair while it's happening.
Last week the creative director said, "Binita, you've been quiet," and I said, "I agree with Avni." I didn't, actually.
Now my name isn't on the new campaign. Of course it isn't. Nobody knows what I think. The silence is making me smaller, and the smaller I get, the more I believe I have nothing to add.

qa.q: What did Binita say when the creative director mentioned the silence?
qa.a: I agree with Avni.

qa.q: What does Binita feel when comparing with Avni in reviews?
qa.a: Binita feels insecure and small, measuring private doubts against how confident everyone else looks from outside.

qa.q: What could break the cycle for Binita?
qa.a: Sharing one of the notebook ideas in the next review, even starting with 'I'm not sure', the way Avni does.

qa.q: How might Avni experience these reviews?
qa.a: Avni may feel unsure too but speaks anyway, and probably doesn't realise Binita has ideas waiting in a notebook.

grounding: A young designer compares inner doubt with colleagues' outer confidence, stays silent, and the invisibility feeds the belief of adding little.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Supervisor's note, lab meeting, 9 October
Sudha has now sat through six lab meetings without speaking. Her bench work is careful; her notebook is the tidiest in the lab. But when we discuss results she looks down at her pad and lets Rekha answer, even about the assay Sudha ran herself.
Today I asked her directly about the odd reading in plate 3. She started, "It might be... no, it's probably nothing," and Rekha finished the thought. I spoke to Sudha afterwards. She said, "Everyone here talks like they've done a PhD already. I don't want to say something silly." She also said she assumed nobody noticed her work anyway.
My worry is the loop: the less she speaks, the less visible her work becomes, and the more she believes it isn't worth much.
Next step: I'll ask her to present plate 3 for five minutes next week, and go through it with her on Monday first.

qa.q: How many lab meetings has Sudha sat through without speaking?
qa.a: Six lab meetings.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she said 'it's probably nothing'?
qa.a: She felt insecure and afraid of sounding silly next to colleagues who seem so sure.

qa.q: What step did the supervisor plan, and why might it help?
qa.a: Asking Sudha to present plate 3 after a practice run on Monday gives her a safe, prepared way to be heard.

qa.q: How might Rekha see Sudha's silence?
qa.a: Rekha may simply see a quiet colleague and step in to help, not realising she is filling a space Sudha wanted to speak into.

grounding: A supervisor notes a capable young researcher who compares herself with confident colleagues, stays silent and grows less visible.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Tuesday.
Another planning meeting, another hour of saying nothing. Naveen talked for ten minutes about the new dashboard like he had invented dashboards. Everyone nodded. I had an idea about the filter problem, a good one I think, but I kept imagining him raising one eyebrow, so I stayed quiet and doodled boxes in my notebook.
Everyone there looks so sure. Meanwhile inside me it's all what if I'm wrong, what if it's obvious, what if it's stupid. Comparing my insides to their outsides, Didi calls it.
The worst part: at the end the manager said, "Saurabh, anything to add?" and I said, "No, all good." Then she gave the filter work to Naveen. Of course. Why wouldn't she? I've been invisible for three months. Now I'm annoyed at myself for being invisible and at them for not seeing me, both at once.

qa.q: What did Saurabh doodle during the meeting?
qa.a: Boxes in a notebook.

qa.q: What feelings does Saurabh have at the end of the meeting?
qa.a: Saurabh feels annoyed at being invisible and frustrated with the others for not noticing, both at once.

qa.q: What small step could help Saurabh at the next meeting?
qa.a: Saurabh could note the idea beforehand and share it early, or send it to the manager afterwards, so silence stops feeding the belief.

qa.q: How might the manager see Saurabh after three months?
qa.a: The manager likely sees someone with nothing to add, so the filter work went to Naveen, not knowing Saurabh had a good idea.

grounding: Shows a newcomer comparing inner doubts with colleagues' outward confidence and staying silent, which makes them less visible and feeds the doubt.
